title: 7 Theses on Formation, Education, and Artificial Intelligence
author: Paul Matthews
summary: Paul Matthews argues that the educational response to AI misuse by students has been framed as a task-design problem — making assignments AI-proof — when the deeper issue is a world-design problem: what kind of educational environment are we building, and what habits of being does it cultivate? Matthews draws on his earlier distinction between 'completion goals' (producing a task) and 'formation goals' (producing a person), arguing that students with completion goals will always find the path of least resistance through AI, while formation goals are more robust. The seven theses address how to construct the educational 'world' within which AI use takes place: rethinking what assessment is for, valuing the struggle of learning itself, making thinking visible, designing tasks where the process matters more than the product, being explicit about the distinction between using AI as a thinking partner versus as a task-outsourcing engine, building trust-based AI conversations with students, and centering the formation question above the compliance question. Matthews writes from a Christian school perspective but the framework is broadly applicable to any educator trying to cultivate genuine learning rather than performative task completion.
points: The shift from 'how do we AI-proof our tasks?' to 'what kind of learners are we forming?' is the article's most important reframe: assessment design cannot solve a formation problem.

Completion-goal students will always find the most efficient path to task production, including AI shortcuts; formation-goal students have an internal reason to engage genuinely that is more durable than any external constraint.

Making thinking visible — through process documentation, verbal explanation, iterative drafts — is the practical answer to the AI-completion problem, because it assesses the thinking rather than the product the thinking produced.

The distinction between AI as a thinking partner (which extends and challenges the student's own reasoning) and AI as a task engine (which bypasses reasoning entirely) needs to be made explicit with students, not assumed.

Matthews's most uncomfortable thesis is that AI misuse is a symptom of an educational model that has historically rewarded task production over genuine intellectual development — AI just makes the underlying incentive problem visible.

It’s about constructing the world within which learning and AI use take place. So as we think about leading our learners to use AI wisely, we don’t start with task design.
If a student is genuinely trying to become something, offloading the work to a machine is self-defeating, and they know it. So what if AI use is primarily a matter of desire, not design?
Not only are students capable of formation-first thinking, they’re already doing it. Think about the student who plays soccer, or the one who practises piano.

We can slip into thinking that if we don’t attend to it, students will at least still complete their tasks, even if they aren’t formed. The only question is whether they’re becoming the sort of person who prioritises task completion, or the sort of person who seeks growth and learning.
What students need to realise is that their education isn’t about a future job. Vocation comes from the Latin root for ‘call’, and learning is their calling right now, not in ten years.

Not that we once learned, back when we did our training, but that we are learning still. Every day we expect our students to walk into our classroom, confront their limitations, and grow through effort.
